rashi:a1.1: And the other [Rav], who derives it from “And their flesh shall be yours…”: that [comparison by itself] certainly speaks of the breast and thigh of a thanks offering. Rather, he derives the two days from “it shall be yours,” which implies another “being” beyond this one.
tosafot:a1.1: One might say: the breast and thigh of a thanks offering: Rabbi Akiva does not accept this reasoning, at the end of Eizehu Mekoman (Zevachim 57a); and it explains there that they disagree about “from it” and something else, whether it counts as a juxtaposition [hekesh] or not.
gershom:a1.1: One could say: the breast and thigh of a thanks offering, which is also [a kind of] peace offering, yet is eaten only for a day and a night.
rashi:a3.1: For we have not found in the entire Torah: that he gives it to the priest, except from the amplification of this “it shall be yours.”
tosafot:a3.1: For we have not found for it in the entire Torah: Rashi explained: that he gives it to the priest, except from the amplification. [But] by his explanation one could say this of every exposition. The Ri explains that this is what it means: we have not found anything like it in the entire Torah, that he gives it entirely [to the priest]. For a sin offering and a guilt offering, which belong to the priest when they are offered on the altar, if they became blemished, then since the altar loses its share, the priest loses too; but a firstborn, even a blemished one, belongs to the priest. And similarly that passage in chapter Shtei Middot (Menachot 91b) about libations, “for the one lamb”: this is the eleventh [animal] of the tithe, “for we have not found in the entire Torah that the secondary is more stringent than the primary,” though one could have said: let the eleventh of the tithe prove [otherwise], as it answers there concerning the leftover of a Passover offering. And similarly in Shabbat, chapter Amar Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 83b): this is the moving of a zav, “for we have not found in the entire Torah that impurity by moving imparts impurity.”
gershom:a2.1: For we have not found in the entire Torah that a blemished firstborn [goes] to the priest, except from here.
rashi:a4.1: And the other [Rav], who derives two days and one night from “it shall be yours”: that a blemished firstborn is given to the priest he derives from “and their flesh,” which is plural: both an unblemished one and a blemished one.
rashi:a4.2: And the other: “and their flesh” implies only unblemished ones, and it uses the plural because it refers to the firstborn of all Israel.
tosafot:a4.1: And the other: “and their flesh” speaks of the firstborn of all Israel: At the end of Eizehu Mekoman (Zevachim 57a), Rabbi Yishmael answers: “and their flesh” speaks of these [firstborn], which means it refers to the firstborn of the ox, the sheep and the goat written just before it; that is a different answer. And if you ask: but the tanna expounds nothing from the plural “and their flesh,” yet in the discussion there earlier (Zevachim 56b) Rabbi Yosei HaGelili expounds: it does not say “its blood” but “their blood,” not “its fat” but “their fat,” teaching about the firstborn and the tithe that they require placement of the blood and of the sacrificial portions on the altar? One can say that this is a dispute, at the beginning of chapter Beit Shammai in Zevachim (37a), and Rabbi Yishmael derives it from “and the blood of your offerings shall be poured out.”
gershom:a3.1: “And their flesh”: it speaks of these firstborn [“But the firstborn of an ox, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat…”], of unblemished ones and not of blemished ones. [An editor’s note: Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading here matches Zevachim 57a; see Tosafot here.]
rashi:a5.1: And after its year also thirty days: even though the blemish developed within its year, long before.
rashi:a5.2: All twelve months: until it is twelve months old from its birth.
rashi:a5.3: Where a blemish developed after its year: he may keep it thirty days from when the blemish developed after its year. And this is what the mishna means: and if the blemish developed after its year, he keeps it thirty days.
rashi:a6.1: In the present time: when an unblemished [firstborn] is fit for nothing.
rashi:a6.2: Before it is fit to be shown to an expert: that no blemish has befallen it, [even] after its year.
tosafot:a6.1: Before it is fit to be shown to an expert: Rashi explained: that no blemish has befallen it. This is difficult: what does “he is permitted to keep it two or three years” mean? He must keep it regardless! And it is forced to explain “permitted” as “obligated,” like that passage in Arakhin (28b): one consecrates it with a consecration of its value, as much as a person would want to give for this offering to make it a burnt offering, even though he is not permitted, which means “even though he is not obligated.” We could explain that it says “permitted to keep it” meaning: and he need not confine it in a cell [to die], even though for other sacred animals that one consecrated or devoted in the present time we say in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (13a): the animal is hamstrung, [or] one locks the door before it and it dies of itself. But that would imply that if he wanted to confine it in a cell he could, and it is an everyday practice that people keep them until a blemish befalls them. It seems [better] to explain “before it is fit to be shown to an expert”: that no expert happened to be available after the blemish befell it, [and] he need not take it far away to the place where the expert is.
gershom:a4.1: Before it is fit to be shown to an expert: that is, before a blemish befalls it, he may keep it two or three years if there is no priest there.
rashi:a7.1: He is not permitted to keep it even one day: it is presently assumed that this refers to a blemish that developed within its year, and it teaches: but due to returning a lost item to the owners, that is, the priest. For perhaps, while this firstborn is in the Israelite’s hands, he will not find a priest to give it to, and if he slaughters it the meat will rot; [so] they said he may keep it thirty days, and if he does not find a priest he slaughters it and salts it until he finds a priest. Evidently the thirty days it mentions refer to a blemish that developed within its year.
tosafot:a7.1: Due to returning a lost item to the owners: Rashi explained: that is, the priest, for sometimes he will not find a priest to give it to, and if he slaughters it at once it will rot; therefore he may keep it thirty days after its year. And Rabbi [Tosafot’s teacher] says that it speaks of [a firstborn] in the priest’s hands who does not need meat now, and the Sages gave him a period of thirty days; but an Israelite always waits until he finds a priest.
gershom:a5.1: And once it is fit to be shown: that is, when a blemish befell it. But due to returning a lost item to the owners they said he may keep it thirty days, for in the meantime perhaps a priest will come; for if he slaughters it earlier, perhaps it will rot before a priest comes.
rashi:a8.1: Still let it be asked: in the baraita itself there is room for doubt. One can say that what it teaches, “after its year he is not permitted to keep it…,” means: if [the blemish] developed after its year he is not permitted to keep it etc., and it is on this that “but due to returning a lost item…” stands.
rashi:a8.2: Or perhaps before its year: that is, if the blemish developed before its year, it also says that after its year [he has] thirty days.
gershom:a6.1: And still let the question be asked about the thirty days: [do they apply to one] that developed a blemish within its year or after its year? For certainly where it developed after its year he may keep it another thirty; but if it developed a blemish earlier, [the question is] whether he may keep it all its year and then thirty more. “One completes for it fifteen days after its year”: evidently one gives him thirty after its blemish, and not thirty after its year, when a blemish befell it within its year.
rashi:a9.1: One completes for it fifteen days after its year: evidently the thirty days the mishna teaches refer to a blemish that developed after its year. For if the blemish developed within its year, even only one day [before its end], one cannot say that we give him thirty days after its year, since he has only the completion, as the baraita teaches. And we learn from it that if the blemish developed within its year, a month or two [before its end], he may keep it until [the end of] its year, since “year” is written; and if the blemish developed after the year, or close to the end of its year, we give him thirty days from when the blemish developed.
gershom:a7.1: But if a blemish developed after its year, one gives him thirty after its year; and if a blemish developed at the beginning of its year, one gives him all its year and no more.
rashi:a9.2: One gives him thirty days: if the blemish developed after its year.
gershom:a8.1: From the time a blemish developed: if a blemish developed at the end of its year.
rashi:a10.1: Year by year: implies two years. Thirty days in a year count as a year, according to all, in the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (10b).
rashi:a11.1: Completion, yes; giving, no: giving him thirty full days, we do not.
gershom:a9.1: Completion, yes; giving, no: that is, we do not give him anything after its year [beyond the completion].
rashi:a12.1: Mishna. And shows its blemish: after the slaughter, and it is found to be permanent.
gershom:a10.1: One who slaughters the firstborn and shows its blemish: that is, after he slaughtered it.
gershom:a11.1: Rabbi Yehuda permits: since he showed it to an expert.
gershom:a12.1: Rabbi Meir says: since it was slaughtered not according to an expert: that is, since he did not show it before the slaughter. Even though he shows it to him after the slaughter and it is a permanent blemish, even so Rabbi Meir penalizes [him], and it is forbidden.
rashi:a13.1: Gemara. Dukin [the cornea]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), as in “who stretches out the heavens like a thin film [dok]” (Isaiah 40:22).
gershom:a13.1: With dukin of the eye: if he shows them after the slaughter, all agree it is forbidden, because they change after death.
tosafot:a13.1: Rabbi Meir holds that we decree [for] blemishes on the body…: And Rabbi [Tosafot’s teacher] says: even though we say at the beginning of Af Al Pi (Ketubot 57a) that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees, this one here is called just below a penalty that Rabbi Meir imposes; and the She’iltot of Rav Aḥai explains that the halakha follows him only in his decrees and not in [his] penalties. And they ruled that the halakha does not follow him in the case of another man’s pregnant or nursing wife, where Rabbi Meir says he must divorce her and never take her back; and the discussion at the beginning of HaḤoletz (Yevamot 37a) does not follow Rabbi Meir. Likewise the discussion here follows Rabbi Yehuda, for according to Rabbi Meir we would penalize in every case on account of those that change; and below, where it asks, “Shall we say we learned the unattributed mishna in accordance with Rabbi Meir?” it answers: perhaps with dukin of the eye, and it is the opinion of all. And so it is in truth. On this basis Rabbi rules not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who penalizes [the lender] in a document that contains interest, that he collects neither the principal nor the interest (Bava Metzia 72a).
rashi:a14.1: They change: because of the pain of death the eye changes; and even though now it looks permanent, had he seen it while it was alive it would have looked passing.
rashi:a14.2: On the body: for example, its ear was split.
rashi:a14.3: Due to those that change: that is, due to the dukin of the eye, which change, [there is] a decree for blemishes on the body, even though they do not change.
gershom:a14.1: Rather, say: due to those that change: the dukin of the eye; for he penalizes [for] blemishes on the body, which do not change, on account of those in the eye.
rashi:b1.1: The mishna is also precise: that they disagree about blemishes on the body, but about dukin they do not disagree.
rashi:b1.2: Since it was slaughtered not according to an expert: for Rabbi Meir finds no flaw in it, only he penalizes him for slaughtering it not according to an expert. Had it been dukin of the eye, it should have taught: Rabbi Meir prohibits because they change. Rather, there is certainly no flaw, since they disagree about blemishes of the body, and he imposes a penalty, a decree on account of dukin.
gershom:b1.1: The mishna is also precise that Rabbi Meir penalizes: for it says, since it was slaughtered not according to an expert, it is forbidden, even though now it is a permanent blemish.
rashi:b2.1: That all of them change: [the question is] whether all dukin of the eye change, or perhaps among the dukin themselves there are some that change and some that do not; but in any case, for blemishes on the body we decree on account of those dukin that change.
rashi:b3.1: What is the practical difference: for even if there are some that do not change, since we do not know which change and which do not, all are forbidden if slaughtered without an expert.
rashi:b3.2: To contradict witnesses: if he slaughtered it without an expert, and now we see it is permanent, and witnesses stand [and testify] that it did not change and that it had this appearance while alive.
rashi:b3.3: They are liars: and it is forbidden according to all.
rashi:b3.4: We rely on them: and it is permitted according to Rabbi Yehuda, who does not penalize.
gershom:b2.1: To contradict witnesses: for example, now after death it appears to be a permanent blemish, and witnesses come and say: we certainly saw it like this before it was slaughtered.
gershom:b3.1: For if you say that all of them change, the witnesses are liars, and the firstborn is forbidden.
gershom:b4.1: Come and I will show you: [that is,] I will teach you.
rashi:b5.1: Unattributed in accordance with Rabbi Meir: who said above, “both this and that are forbidden”; for it teaches “it must be buried,” even though now it looks permanent.
gershom:b5.1: Shall we say we learned the unattributed mishna in accordance with Rabbi Meir: that is, that even though now, after the slaughter, it appears a complete blemish, even so it must be buried; that is like Rabbi Meir, who penalizes.
rashi:b5.2: Perhaps with dukin of the eye: [there] it said “it must be buried,” since according to all they change.
gershom:b6.1: No, with dukin of the eye, and it is the opinion of all: that is why it must be buried, since they change.
rashi:b6.1: When he pays: to the priest, he gives a quarter of its value for the firstborn of a small animal, and for the firstborn of a large animal half its value. He pays half because it is money whose ownership is in doubt. For one can say that he caused the loss of all of it: had he not permitted it this way, [the owner] would have brought it before a full expert, who would have permitted it, and [the priest] would have eaten it, and now it requires burial. And one can say that he caused no loss at all: perhaps it was not a blemish and a full expert would not have permitted it, and perhaps a permanent blemish would never have befallen it until it died.
tosafot:b6.1: A quarter for a small animal and half for a large one: And although Rashi explained that it is because it is money whose ownership is in doubt, [since] perhaps an expert would permit it for the blemish and perhaps he would not, this is not because it follows Sumakhos; rather, it is merely an enactment of the Sages. And even though it speaks of any blemish, even one where it is known that an expert would permit it on its account, he still considers it somewhat in doubt, for perhaps an expert would not attend to it; and also [the baraita] makes no distinction between blemishes. Had this baraita spoken specifically of dukin of the eye, it would sit better, since we hold like Rabbi Yehuda, as I explained, and according to him it is buried only for dukin of the eye. One can also explain that this is why he pays half: the Sages estimated that it is worth no more as long as it stands in doubt and has not yet been permitted. With teruma, too, we find that it is worth only about half of non-sacred produce, as we say in chapter Af Al Pi (Ketubot 58a): wherever teruma is mentioned, he gives her double in non-sacred food. But it is not truly like teruma, which is forbidden to non-priests and forbidden in impurity, whereas a blemished firstborn is entirely permitted, like a deer or a gazelle.
gershom:b7.1: He pays a quarter for a small animal. And some say: that is why he pays half and not more, since it is money whose ownership is in doubt, as there are dukin that do not change. (The text has an unclear abbreviation here; an editor’s note suggests reading: “And some say that he pays half for a large animal because we say…”, referring to Bava Batra 146b.) And half for a large one [the printed text reads “for the Most High,” apparently a slip], because we say that he pays the value of the meat at a cheap price.
rashi:b6.2: What is the reason: [for] a quarter for a small animal and half for a large one?
gershom:b8.1: What is the reason: for this half.
rashi:b6.3: A large animal, its loss is great: therefore the payment is great.
gershom:b9.1: For this one, a large animal, he causes it great loss; therefore he pays much: half.
gershom:b10.1: And this one: a small animal, whose loss is small since it is not so big, he pays a quarter.
rashi:b7.1: Let him pay according to the loss: to this one half of its larger value, and to that one half of its smaller value.
gershom:b11.1: If its loss is small, let him pay according to its loss: that is, half of that small [value]. Why is it different, [that he pays] a quarter?
rashi:b7.2: They touched upon it due to the decree on those who raise small livestock: due to the trouble of those who raise small livestock, for raising it is a great trouble; and this one who permitted the firstborn saved the priest from great trouble, for perhaps had [the owner] shown it to another, he would not have permitted it, and he would have had much more care [of it] until a blemish befell it. Therefore they touched upon it, so that he pays only a quarter. Another version: due to the decree on those who raise small livestock, who transgress the words of the Sages, as we learned (Bava Kamma 79b): one may not raise small livestock in the Land of Israel; the Sages penalized him so that he takes only a quarter. (Rashi adds: and not from the teacher’s mouth, [i.e., he did not receive this second version from his teacher].)
tosafot:b7.1: Due to the decree on those who raise small livestock: that is, the Sages were strict with them not to raise them except in woodlands outside settled areas, and this involves great trouble, and it is worth only a quarter, which is half as much as the large animal. Rashi too explained that they decreed it because of the trouble, but he did not take care to account for the word “decree.”
gershom:b12.1: Due to the penalty on those who raise small livestock: for it is forbidden to raise small livestock in the Land of Israel. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s heading reads “penalty” where our text reads “decree.”]
gershom:b13.1: And we are dealing with a case where this firstborn is from a priest’s animal, and he raised the small livestock.
tosafot:b8.1: He judged the case…: In the first chapter of Sanhedrin (6a) it raises an objection from this against Rabbi Abbahu, who said: two who judged, their judgment is no judgment. And it is puzzling: from where does it know that this speaks of a single judge? If because it teaches “he judged the case” in the singular, at the beginning of Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 44b) it teaches “he judged the case” and does not speak of a single [judge], as it teaches, “and all of them may buy.” One can say that there it is taught in parallel with witnesses, but the mishna here speaks entirely of a single [judge], as the latter clause teaches, “And if he was an expert for the court…,” and “an incident with Rabbi Tarfon…,” and the first clause too: “one who is not an expert and examined the firstborn.”
rashi:b8.1: Mishna. And if he was an expert for the court, he is exempt: for [the litigant] cannot say to him: Why did you judge me, since you are not versed in the laws?
gershom:b14.1: And if he was an expert: for the public, who erred only in deliberation, he is exempt from paying.
rashi:b9.1: Gemara. Rabbi Meir, who judges [liability for] indirect damage: in Bava Kamma, chapter HaGozel Etzim (Bava Kamma 100a): a vineyard’s partition that was breached, [and the owner of the field] says to him: Fence it; he gave up on it and did not fence it: he has rendered [the grain] forbidden and is liable for it. Indirect damage, for he caused his fellow’s grain to become forbidden.
tosafot:b9.1: Shall we say we learned the unattributed mishna in accordance with Rabbi Meir…: It is puzzling that it does not infer here from the first clause, “one who is not an expert and examined the firstborn and it was slaughtered on his ruling, it must be buried and he pays from his house.” That, whichever way you look at it, follows Rabbi Meir, who judges indirect damage, since it cannot be explained as [where] he took and gave with his hand, as it teaches “it was slaughtered on his ruling.” And in HaGozel Kamma (Bava Kamma 100a) it finds no mishna where Rabbi Meir judges indirect damage, only the baraita of the vineyard’s partition; it should have cited this one. And in HaGozel Batra (Bava Kamma 117b), concerning that man who pointed out [another’s property], where he wanted to hold him liable from the mishna “he judged the case” and it was rejected, why did he not hold him liable from this one?
gershom:b15.1: Who judges indirect damage: in Bava Kamma, chapter HaGozel Etzim. And this one causes the loss of money by his speech.
gershom:b16.1: Where he took and gave with his hand: he took with his own hands from this one and gave to that one; he is not [merely] a cause but a robber.
rashi:b10.1: Granted, he found an innocent party liable, one finds it where he took and gave with his hand: he himself took the money from him with his hand and paid the litigant.
rashi:b10.2: But he exempted a liable party, what are the circumstances: perforce you cannot find that he did anything; he only said to him: You are exempt.
rashi:b10.3: That he had collateral: [that is,] the lender; and this [judge] exempted the borrower and took the collateral from the lender’s hand and returned it to the borrower.
gershom:b17.1: For example, where the defendant’s collateral was in the plaintiff’s hand, and he took it from him and gave it to this one.
rashi:b11.1: That he had a creeping animal touch them: they brought foodstuffs before him to ask about them, and he said they are impure, and he took a creeping animal and touched them with it, so that there would be no more doubt about them, and to uphold his words.
gershom:b18.1: That he had a creeping animal touch them: with his hands.
rashi:b11.2: That he mixed them with his produce: [the questioner] brought foodstuffs before him to ask about them, and he said they are pure, and he himself took them and mixed them with the produce of the one who asked. In the end an expert sage said they are impure, and they made impure the rest with which they were mixed.
gershom:b19.1: He declared the impure pure: for example, he took impure produce and said they are pure, and mixed them with his fellow’s produce; he acted with his hands and caused the loss of his produce.
rashi:b12.2: And Rabbi Tarfon fed it to the dogs: for they asked him about it, whether it is a tereifa, and he fed it to the dogs.
gershom:b21.1: And fed it to the dogs: for he said that it is a tereifa.
rashi:b13.1: So that it will not give birth: because their cows and sows are very superior and they sell them dearly, and they want them not to give birth in another kingdom, so that [others] will need them. They cut out its womb and it does not die; therefore it is not a tereifa.
rashi:b14.1: Your donkey is gone, Tarfon: you have lost a donkey, which you will pay to the owner of the cow.
gershom:b22.1: Your donkey is gone, Tarfon: that is, you have lost your donkey; that is, you will pay him your donkey in place of his cow that you caused him to lose.
rashi:b15.1: Gemara. And let him derive it: that even if he were not an expert he would be exempt, since he erred in a matter [stated in a] mishna, as we learned in Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 54a): if the womb was removed, it is kosher; and one who errs in a matter [stated in a] mishna retracts, in Sanhedrin (33a). And since, had the cow still existed, he could have retracted and permitted it, it turns out that what he said is nothing, and this one who fed it to the dogs caused the loss to himself.
gershom:b23.1: And let him derive: that he is exempt from paying, because one who errs in a matter [stated in a] mishna retracts, for we learned: if its womb was removed, it is kosher.
rashi:b16.1: Alternatively, you erred in deliberation: where even if it still existed you could not retract and permit it, so your prohibition stands as a prohibition and you caused the loss; even so you are exempt from paying, since you are an expert. Deliberation is explained in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (6a): for example, two Tannaim or two Amoraim who disagree, and the halakha was not stated like either, and the general practice follows one of them, and this one went and acted like the other: what he did is done, and he pays from his house.
rashi:b17.1: Mishna. One may not slaughter: lest he permit it for the sake of the fee.
gershom:b24.1: One may not slaughter on his ruling: for one could say that he permits it because of the fee he takes.
